alignment.note: Greek opens with καί followed by a genitive absolute participle (ἐκπορευομένου); the Vulgate renders the temporal clause with et cum + imperfect subjunctive (egrederetur), and the Peshitta with the compound conjunction ܘܟܕ ('and when'). The constructions are equivalent in sense but the Greek participial absolute is reframed as a finite subordinate clause in both versions.

Greek and Vulgate carry the pronominal subject (αὐτοῦ / encoded in egrederetur), whereas the Peshitta makes the subject explicit by naming ܝܫܘܥ ('Jesus'), a common Syriac clarifying tendency to specify pronominal referents at the head of a pericope.
ἱεροῦ / ܗܝܟܠܐ / templo; the parenthetical transliteration (hi'erou) attaches to the Greek noun and carries no semantic weight.

Greek expresses the partitive genitive plural μαθητῶν + possessive αὐτοῦ ('of his disciples'); the Vulgate renders the possessor with a separate adjective suis, while the Peshitta fuses the noun and the third-person possessive suffix into a single form ܬܠܡܝܕܘܗܝ. The difference is purely morphological, reflecting each language's manner of marking possession.
διδάσκαλε / ܡܠܦܢܐ / Magister, the vocative address 'Teacher/Master'.

The single Greek interjection ἴδε ('behold') is matched by the Vulgate's imperative aspice ('look'), but the Peshitta employs a hendiadys of ܗܐ ('behold') plus ܚܙܝ ('see'), doubling the attention-marker — a characteristic Syriac amplification of deictic particles.
ποταποὶ / ܐܝܠܝܢ / quales, the exclamatory/interrogative 'what (sort of)!'.

The Greek repeats the full exclamatory pronoun ποταπαὶ (feminine) before the second noun, and the Vulgate likewise repeats quales; the Peshitta economises by prefixing the conjunction ܘ directly to a single repeated interrogative ܘܐܝܠܝܢ, here grouped with the conjunction (idx 15) so that the second exclamatory force is carried compactly.
οἰκοδομαί / ܒܢܝܢܐ / structuræ, 'buildings'; the Greek paragraph mark (¶) is a formatting glyph without textual import.

The Greek mid-verse high point (·) after αὐτοῦ and the Vulgate colon (:) both mark the onset of direct speech; the Peshitta supplies no graphic punctuation, relying on syntax alone to introduce the disciple's address.
